cards.title: Topgrading interviews: chronological deep-dive by role
cards.summary: Run a topgrading interview that walks each résumé role chronologically and stress-tests title vs. actual scope, wins, lows, manager and exit reasons.
cards.use_when: Hiring for an ecommerce role with real budget or P&L impact — head of procurement, paid media buyer, supply chain lead, COO — where a wrong hire is expensive and résumé titles can inflate scope.
steps: Before the interview, list every role on the CV in order. For each one, ask what the candidate was actually hired to do versus the title they held (e.g., 'you were titled managing director but hired as entrepreneur-in-residence — what did the job start as, and what did it take to progress?').
For each role ask four consistent questions: biggest point of pride, low points, who they reported to and worked with, and why they left.

Convert the reference question into a trap for inflated claims: ask what their manager's name was, then 'if I called [name], how would they rate you 1–10?' Screening usually only allows checking the last manager; topgrading lets you probe every role on a long CV.
Use the answers to filter for candidates aligned to your organizational goals, not just skill match — mismatch shows up in how they describe culture, lows and exits.
Expect the process to feel unusually granular. Roman reports the right candidates appreciate the depth because it signals how thoughtfully the company is run.
caveats: Topgrading is time-intensive and only pays off for roles where a bad hire is costly; it is overkill for low-impact hires.
Manager-rating questions put candidates on the spot deliberately — treat evasiveness as data, but confirm claims with actual reference calls before deciding.

cards.title: Five-step funnel with a ~1% hiring acceptance rate
cards.summary: Structure hiring as scorecard, screening, topgrading, competency/culture and offer, and expect roughly 1% of applicants to receive an offer.
cards.use_when: Building a repeatable hiring pipeline for a growing ecommerce operation, or deciding how much screening effort a role justifies.
steps: Step 1 — scorecard: define the role's outcomes up front and have candidates apply through the website against it. In Roman's process roughly 70% are filtered out at this stage (about 30 of 100 applicants reach screening).
Step 2 — screening: a phone call that filters further, with about 70–80% rejection at this stage in his experience, leaving roughly 20 of the original 100.
Step 3 — topgrading: chronologically walk every role on the CV (see separate topgrading card).
Step 4 — competency and culture: run a case study for competency plus basic cultural-fit questions; this is where the operating rhythm is pressure-tested.
Step 5 — offer: from about 20 surviving candidates, extend a maximum of one offer. Result is roughly a 1% applicant-to-offer rate.
Keep headcount lean rather than hiring ahead of the curve: Roman deliberately runs near-zero excess capacity and hires only when utilization is tight, to protect opex.
caveats: These percentages are Roman's own reported funnel, not a benchmark to hit; smaller roles may not justify all five steps.
Running deliberately understaffed is his stated preference for opex and utilization — weigh against burnout and delivery risk in your store.

cards.title: Hire specialized roles in low-cost hubs, not US generalists
cards.summary: Salary arbitrage (roughly $100k US vs $20–30k Shenzhen vs ~$10k Philippines) works for specialized roles that need less cross-functional context.
steps: Map each open role as specialist or generalist. Roman's rule: if it's specialized and doesn't need broad multifunctional context — e.g., procurement, BI/analytics, PPC — a low-cost overseas hub can deliver comparable output. If it's a broad generalist doing five things, US hiring may make more sense.
Benchmark cost: he cites ~$100k US salary as roughly $20k–30k/year in Shenzhen and about $10k in the Philippines, with Shenzhen around 2x Philippines cost.

Prioritize Shenzhen for high-caliber specialist work: he reports its talent caliber is very high and cites Shenzhen-based D2C companies doing nine figures, one growing from $10M to $100M to a reported $500M, plus strong work ethic and consistency.
Treat the arbitrage as protecting margin of error — lower cost base lets you keep investing in people and paid media rather than draining opex.
Before committing, verify current wage levels and hiring/visa realities for your target hub; salary comparisons shift over time.
caveats: Roman notes specialized roles translate well; generalist roles needing broad context are where he says US hiring still fits.
The cited company revenue figures are anecdotes, not typical outcomes, and he explicitly avoids naming those companies.

cards.title: In-house vs agency: keep marketing in-house pre-$50M
cards.summary: If you're a sub-$50M brand, Roman argues you're winning on unique product or marketing savviness — so never outsource marketing if you're good at it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to hand paid media, creative or growth to an agency versus building it in-house at a small-to-mid ecommerce brand.
steps: Diagnose why your store is winning: Roman's frame is that sub-$50M businesses win either through a unique product with strong USPs, through marketing savviness, or both.

If marketing is your edge, keep it in-house. He states that if you're good at marketing, never outsource it, and that pre-nine-figures revenue he's rarely seen a good marketer delegate the marketing division successfully.
Control your biggest cost line directly — he names marketing as his biggest cost and wants to hold the reins on it, even while each company has a professional CEO.
For reference, he operates essentially 100% in-house rather than using agencies.
If you're not the marketing savant, that still leaves product differentiation as the winning lever — invest budget and attention there instead of assuming agencies will fix growth.
caveats: This is Roman's founder-driven opinion tied to sub-$50M businesses; it isn't a universal rule against agencies, and he acknowledges the choice depends on the founder's own skills.

cards.title: Fire C players without triggering A-player panic
cards.summary: Before mass layoffs, pre-brief your A players one-on-one so they don't read the cuts as a signal to leave.
cards.use_when: Cutting headcount or restructuring a store team, especially when layoffs are visible and top performers may interpret them as instability.
steps: Before the layoffs, take each A player out individually for a coffee or private conversation.
Tell them directly: we're not doing well, we're going to fix it, but we have to make difficult cuts. You're safe, you'll see colleagues leave, and if you stay we'll take care of you.
Only then let the underperformers go. Roman's biggest regretted mistake at Rocket Internet's Zalora was mass-firing C players before talking to A players, causing panic and losing top people.
His framing for the player tiers (attributed to Marc Samwer): any organization has a maximum ~10% A players and roughly 60% B players, with the rest C — a reputed heuristic, not a measurable formula.

A related litmus test from How to Make a Few Billion: a C player resigning should feel like 'I don't care,' a B player like 'eh,' and you should never be blindsided by an A player leaving. Keep A players pre-informed.
Also apply the inverse when selling: run reference calls on the acquirer so you don't sell your company to someone you can't work with.
caveats: The 10%/60% player split is a quoted heuristic from the Samwer brothers, not a measured benchmark; treat it as directional.
Pre-briefing A players only works if you actually follow through with the promised support after the cuts.

cards.title: Acquisition lens: only two levers — marketing spend and bill of materials
cards.summary: When evaluating a business to buy, ask where you have an unfair advantage in paid marketing spend or COGS renegotiation; a neglected ad account is a green field.
cards.use_when: Sourcing or underwriting an ecommerce acquisition, or deciding which existing store asset to buy into based on where you can add the most value.
steps: Ask two questions only: do I have an unfair advantage in marketing, and do I have an unfair advantage in bill of materials (COGS)? Skip other repair areas until these are answered.

Marketing test: is the target spending as much as you think it should on Meta, and is it spending anything at all on influencer? If under-spending on Meta and spending nothing on influencer, that's a green field for an operator who is strong on paid.
Example he cites: a company bought in 2024 ran about $1M/year in ad spend on roughly $24M/year in revenue — the low spend rate was the opportunity, not the warning sign.

BOM test: check optimization levers directly. He asks whether he can add meaningful bottom-line profit by renegotiating terms, and probes whether a 10-year-old business has ever seen its COGS decline — if never, he assumes there's room to negotiate.
Size the thesis as a CAC exercise: can you push spend from, say, $1M toward $10M and hold unit economics? Verify that before committing.
caveats: The $1M spend / $24M revenue company is a specific example, not a typical multiple or a promise of what scaling spend will return.
Low ad spend can reflect a demand ceiling rather than underexploitation — test CAC at higher spend before underwriting it as headroom.

cards.title: Earn the right to buy: lead with value and design a call option
cards.summary: De-risk an acquisition by taking over the founder's marketing budget or spending your own money first, with a written right to buy shares if it works.
cards.use_when: Approaching a founder-owned ecommerce brand you want to acquire or buy into, when you need proof and trust before a large purchase price.
steps: Start small: Roman first bought 12% of Nutrition Kitchen and later owned around 60%, with the founder rolling over equity.
Lead with value instead of offering a large cheque — he initially managed the brand's marketing budget and negotiated a call option: if he scaled the budgets, he had the right to buy more shares.

Alternative test-drive structure he suggests: offer to take over the company's marketing for a month, spending ~$100k of your own money with no strings attached. If you drive revenue, you get the right to buy at a pre-agreed price; if not, the founder keeps the $100k and owes nothing.
Frame the economics: a $100k test is cheaper than a $20–30M acquisition that turns out wrong.
Use the interim period to watch how the founder operates before committing — it functions as a low-cost drive of the car before you buy it.
caveats: The $100k figure and the call-option structure are Roman's own examples; he notes he hasn't executed the exact 'take over for a month' version recently.
Structure the right-to-buy terms in writing up front — the source describes deal terms, not legal templates.

cards.title: Founder red flags: avoid bad actors regardless of price
cards.summary: Roman's top acquisition filter is character: don't buy from — or sell to — someone you can't work with, even on great terms, because it never works out.
cards.use_when: Evaluating founders during acquisition talks, partnership discussions or supplier relationship decisions, especially when the numbers look attractive but people feel off.
steps: Apply the blunt filter: if the person is someone you would never want to deal with, pass — he argues a great deal cannot survive a bad person.

Give the counterparty a confidence check: when he bought a company in June, he offered to let the seller do reference calls on him with his past partners to see what selling to or working with him is like.
Mirror it on your side — run reverse-reference diligence as the seller too, so you don't sell your company to someone you can't work with.
When forced to choose between a great brand with a mediocre founder and a mediocre brand with a great founder, he picks the great brand: it wins over time.
Treat nearly everything else as situational noise once the character filter is passed — terms and red flags are otherwise deal-specific.
caveats: Character judgment is subjective and stated as his strong opinion, not a rule; the brand-versus-founder answer is his stated preference, not a universal law.
He notes there may be facts that never surface — a brand can have a talent you can't see on paper.

cards.title: Use a five-slide recovery deck when negotiating to fix a bad hole
cards.summary: Roman's personal network deck to exit $3M in debt: acknowledge fault, explain the cause, state the plan, give a timeline and payback, then make the ask.
cards.use_when: Facing a serious cash shortfall in your ecommerce business — inventory overbuying, a failed product bet, or a debt hole — and needing capital or support from investors, partners or friends.
steps: Slide 1 — accountability: state plainly that you made the mistake ('I'm an idiot'). Don't spin the situation.
Slide 2 — diagnosis: explain exactly what happened and what led to the hole, in plain terms.
Slide 3 — plan: state how you are going to get out of it, with specifics.
Slide 4 — timeline: give a recovery timeline and a payback window so the counterparty can price the risk.
Slide 5 — the ask: state the specific amount you need and exactly what you're willing to give in return.
Keep it short: five slides, not a data room. The deck's purpose is to make the recovery plan and payback credible.
caveats: The slide outline is Roman's telling of his own turnaround, not a template that guarantees funds; it depends on track record and counterparty trust.
This is an anecdote about raising from personal contacts, not an investment process.

cards.title: Longevity as a category tailwind for the next decade
cards.summary: Roman's answer to 'what new brand would you launch tomorrow' is health and longevity, because he sees the cycle as still at the beginning.
cards.use_when: Choosing a category or new brand direction for an ecommerce product launch, or evaluating whether to double down on an existing health-adjacent line.
steps: Shortlist health and longevity products first when selecting a new category — he says he'd confidently tell a founder to work on it for a decade because the cycle is still early.
Treat tailwinds as category selection input, not a substitute for the product/USP work: his own framing is that sub-$50M winners have a unique product or marketing edge.
Pair the category with a specific operator advantage — e.g., procurement renegotiation or an under-exploited paid channel — so the tailwind is converted into margin and growth.
Do not read the tailwind as a timing guarantee; validate demand and unit economics as you would for any category.
caveats: This is his opinion about category attractiveness, not a forecast or benchmark, and he offers no data on category-level conversion or costs.

cards.title: Near-supplier location builds terms and iteration speed
cards.summary: Being geographically close to your manufacturer (e.g., Hong Kong for China sourcing) increases interaction frequency, which he argues speeds brand growth and unlocks better terms over time.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to base a China-reliant ecommerce operation, or planning supplier management visits and negotiation cadence for a product brand.
steps: Treat supplier proximity as an operating input: if you make products in China or Asia, he argues more time spent with your supplier means more growth — citing interaction frequency as the mechanism.
Use repeat face time to build guanxi (relationship) so you can negotiate terms over time, which he frames as an unfair advantage in an increasingly red-ocean ecommerce market.

Weigh secondary practical factors he cites for Hong Kong: free healthcare, lower rent than New York for comparable space (he cites around $5,000/month for a two- to three-bedroom in a Brooklyn-equivalent area), low taxes, nature, and a strong ecommerce community.
Verify current costs, visa rules and taxes before relocating — the cited figures are point-in-time.
caveats: The rent, salary and quality-of-life figures are the source's rough, point-in-time comparisons, not current market data.
The guanxi payoff is asserted from his experience, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Always be retaining, not just always be selling
cards.summary: Treat retention of top performers as a continuous discipline: pre-brief them on change, keep them informed before surprises, and never be blindsided by an A player resigning.
cards.use_when: Managing key ecommerce staff through growth, restructuring, budget cuts or channel pivots where uncertainty could push strong people out the door.
steps: Adopt the posture 'always be retaining' alongside 'always be selling' — retention is active work, not silence.
Share the hard news before it leaks: Roman's cohost frames the mass-layoff lesson as telling people what's coming rather than letting them discover it.

Use the resignation test from How to Make a Few Billion: if an A player resigns and you're panicking, you failed to see it coming; if a C player resigns and you don't care, that's expected. Aim never to be blindsided by an A player.
Run pre-briefs and check-ins consistently rather than only during crises (see the layoff-prebrief card).
When things stabilize, connect retention back to comp and growth paths — Roman's rule is to keep opex lean but be able to spend on the people who carry the business.
caveats: In his words, better to have a seat empty than filled with the wrong person — the bar for keeping someone is high, and retention of A players is the priority, not headcount.

cards.title: When understaffed is the deliberate plan
cards.summary: Roman explicitly runs lean, near-zero excess capacity and hires only when seams show — a stated opex-first stance, not a universal default.
cards.use_when: Setting headcount and hiring plans for a lean ecommerce operation, especially when deciding whether to add roles ahead of demand.
steps: Adopt the policy he states for Peak21: do not hire ahead of the curve; keep utilization high and avoid excess capacity in any form.
Use understaffing as the trigger: run slightly lean and hire when the team is visibly at the seams, not when a role might someday be needed.
Tie this to the opex argument — lower fixed cost keeps margin of error wider, which he links to being able to spend on people and paid media.
Combine with the specialist lens: add high-utilization specialist roles (procurement, paid media, BI) before adding broad generalist headcount.
caveats: This is his strong stated preference; a deliberate under-capacity policy can harm service levels, delivery or retention if pushed too far.

cards.title: Intensity and tenacity as the founder filter
cards.summary: Asked for the single trait winners share, Roman names intensity and tenacity — use it as a screen when evaluating founders to back, partner with or supply.
cards.use_when: Screening founders for acquisition, partnership or investment in an ecommerce brand, or when assessing whether a supplier or partner will push through hard stretches.
steps: Use intensity and tenacity as the primary trait filter when evaluating founders, ahead of pedigree or polish.
Combine it with the character filter — he also refuses to work with people he can't deal with, even on excellent terms.
Look for persistence behaviors that survive setbacks rather than one-off wins; he tells of quitting school, surviving a failed venture and rebuilding after $3M of debt.
Weigh it against the less glamorous reality: he describes himself as having a gambler streak and says it hurts — intensity can cut both ways in a founder or operator.
caveats: This is a stated opinion from a single operator; intensity without judgment or capital discipline can be destructive, as his own debt history shows.

cards.title: Picks-and-shovels economics of ecommerce penetration
cards.summary: Roman's structural view: ecommerce is a multi-trillion industry growing from ~21–22% of US retail toward a much higher share, but D2C brand billionaires are rare — the infrastructure players capture the scale.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to position an ecommerce business long-term — brand, retailer or infrastructure/supporting layer — based on where value accrues in the industry.
steps: Take the structural view he cites: US ecommerce is roughly 21–22% of all retail (including Amazon) and he argues it could reach around 60% by the time today's children are grown — a long runway for stores and brands.

Note the pattern he highlights: rare D2C-founder billionaires, while picks-and-shovels players (Shopify, Amazon, Pinterest, Snapchat, Klaviyo-type infrastructure) capture enormous scale. Shopify he projects toward $550–600B GMV and Amazon far larger.
If evaluating a brand, weigh the physical/omnichannel path too — he references Pandora at ~$4.5B revenue and ~$1.1B EBITDA with ~2,400 stores as evidence a store-network scale outcome has precedent.
Use this as portfolio logic, not a forecast: for a single store, focus on the two acquisition levers you can actually pull (marketing spend and BOM).
caveats: These figures are the source's rough conversational estimates, some of which he hedges ('don't quote me on this'), not verified data.
The billion-dollar store-network outcome is a long-horizon ambition he says he's uncertain about pursuing, not a plan.
